agent-architecture:
Anthropic's own framing: workflows orchestrate models and tools through predefined code paths you control. Agents let the model direct its own process and tool use at runtime.

◆The decision rule

Choose a workflow when the steps are knowable in advance. Choose an agent only when the number and order of steps genuinely cannot be known. Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution and add complexity only when needed, which sometimes means not building an agentic system at all. Distractors will offer an elegant multi-agent design where a prompt chain is correct.

The five workflow patterns

PatternUse when
Prompt chainingFixed sequential steps, each output feeding the next
RoutingDistinct input categories need different handling. Classify, then dispatch
ParallelizationSectioning for independent subtasks; voting for confidence on the same task
Orchestrator-workersSubtasks determined at runtime by a central model
Evaluator-optimizerClear criteria exist and iteration measurably improves output

Hierarchies and subagents

A manager holds the goal and delegates to specialists; the manager owns decomposition and synthesis. Every hop costs tokens and latency, and errors compound across layers.

✦Why subagents exist

Context isolation, primarily. Each subagent gets its own window, so 50k tokens of raw search results never pollute the parent — only the summary returns. Parallelism is secondary. If an option frames parallelism as the main reason, it's the distractor.
agent-construction-with-claude:
The loop: model receives goal and tools → emits a tool call → your harness executes it → result returns as a tool_result → repeat until it stops calling tools. Your harness owns execution, error handling, iteration limits, and the stop condition.

▲Never forget this

The model never executes anything. It emits a tool_use block describing what it wants. Your code decides whether to run it. This single fact underpins the entire security model and shows up in three separate domains.

Claude Agent SDK

Ships as claude-agent-sdk (Python) and @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk (TypeScript). Formerly the Claude Code SDK, which is why its hook events and permission model mirror Claude Code exactly.

agent.py — Agent SDK with least privilege and a blocking hook
# pip install claude-agent-sdk
import anyio
from claude_agent_sdk import (query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ClaudeSDKClient,
                              tool, create_sdk_mcp_server, HookMatcher)

# --- one-shot ---
async def simple():
    options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Bash"],    # LEAST PRIVILEGE
        system_prompt="You are a careful refactoring assistant.",
        setting_sources=["project"],   # v0.1.0+ no longer loads these by default
    )
    async for message in query(prompt="Fix the bug in auth.py", options=options):
        print(message)

# --- in-process tool + a hook that actually blocks ---
@tool("lookup_order", "Look up an order by ID", {"order_id": str})
async def lookup_order(args):
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": fetch(args["order_id"])}]}

async def block_destructive(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    cmd = input_data["tool_input"].get("command", "")
    if input_data["tool_name"] == "Bash" and "rm -rf" in cmd:
        return {"hookSpecificOutput": {
            "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
            "permissionDecision": "deny",
            "permissionDecisionReason": "Recursive delete blocked by policy"}}
    return {}

server = create_sdk_mcp_server(name="ops", version="1.0.0", tools=[lookup_order])
options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Bash"],
    mcp_servers={"ops": server},
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="Bash", hooks=[block_destructive])]},
)

anyio.run(simple)
// npm i @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk
import { query } from '@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk';

for await (const message of query({
  prompt: 'What files are in this directory?',
  options: {
    allowedTools: ['Bash', 'Glob'],     // LEAST PRIVILEGE
    settingSources: ['project'],
  },
})) {
  console.log(message);
}

// Package was renamed: claude-code-sdk -> claude-agent-sdk,
// ClaudeCodeOptions -> ClaudeAgentOptions.
// A PreToolUse deny holds even under bypassPermissions.
◈Two SDK gotchas

Connecting an MCP server does not by itself let the agent call its tools. You must permit them explicitly via the allow-list.

Since v0.1.0 the SDK no longer loads Claude Code's system prompt and filesystem settings by default. Add setting_sources=["project"] to restore the old behaviour.

Deployment models

  • Self-hosted — you run the harness. Full control over data flow, network, secrets. Required when data residency or network isolation is named.
  • Anthropic-hosted — less operational burden, faster to ship, less control over the execution environment.

Pick by the constraint in the stem: residency and isolation push self-hosted; speed and low ops push managed.
agent-patterns-and-frameworks:
Tool-use loop — always bound it: max iterations, wall-clock timeout, token budget. An unbounded loop is a harness design failure, not a model failure.

Memory

The API is stateless and re-reads everything each turn. Short-term memory is the conversation itself. Long-term memory is an external store you write and read deliberately. Memory is something you design and manage, not something the model has.

Context-window management in agents

Long runs accumulate tool results relentlessly. Anthropic's cookbook names three primitives: compaction (summarize history at a threshold), tool-result clearing (drop old outputs), and memory (persistent files). Plus subagent isolation.

Frameworks

FrameworkShape
LangGraphGraph orchestration, explicit nodes and edges, controllable stateful workflows
PydanticAIPython-native, type-safe agents with Pydantic validation on structured output
StrandsModel-driven agent SDK, minimal scaffolding around the loop

Frameworks buy scaffolding and cost you a layer of abstraction between you and the failure. Start direct; add one when the scaffolding earns its keep.
understanding-requirements:
Translating business requirements into functional requirements (what it must do) and infrastructure requirements (throughput, latency budget, availability, residency, retention, which vendor endpoint).

◆The exam pattern

Every stem contains one buried constraint that determines the answer. Everything else is texture. Train yourself to find it, and read each stem twice.

Constraint in the stemImplication
"not needed until tomorrow"Batch API
"user is waiting"Streaming, latency-optimized tier
"must stay in region X"Regional endpoints or self-hosted
"feeds another system"Structured output + validation
"regulated / high stakes"Human review gate, audit logging
"deterministic rule"Don't use an LLM at all
"reusable across applications"MCP server
"must happen every time"A hook

Solution architecture

Named in this objective alongside functional and infrastructure requirements. It is the bridge artefact: given the business need and the constraints, what components exist and how do they connect? For a Claude system that means naming which model tier sits where, whether calls are realtime or batched, where tools and MCP servers live, where untrusted content enters, where human review gates sit, and which datastore holds session and memory state. If a stem asks you to choose a component, it is asking a solution-architecture question, not a coding one.
systems-life-cycle:
▲Don't over-specialize

The objective scopes this as generic IT systems lifecycle management, not LLM-specific delivery. Standard concepts and frameworks applied to a Claude system.

Plan → develop → test → deploy → operate → maintain → retire.

Frameworks by name

FrameworkFit for LLM work
WaterfallPoor. Model behaviour can't be fully specified up front
Agile / ScrumGood. Matches prompt-and-eval iteration
DevOps / CI-CDGood, with evals as a release gate alongside tests
ITILWhere model migrations and prompt changes become change records

A stem naming change management, release gates, or incident and problem management points at ITIL-shaped service management, not at the coding workflow.

The three Claude-specific wrinkles

  1. Model deprecation is a scheduled lifecycle event. Plan migrations around it.
  2. Prompts are versioned artifacts under change control.
  3. Regression testing requires evals because output is non-deterministic.
claude-api-mechanics:
Messages

basic.py — the four things every question here tests
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a concise assistant.",   # top-level, NOT a message role
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, Claude"}],
)

# content is a LIST OF BLOCKS. Never index [0] blindly.
for block in msg.content:
    if block.type == "text":
        print(block.text)

print(msg.stop_reason)   # end_turn | max_tokens | tool_use | stop_sequence | refusal
print(msg.usage.input_tokens, msg.usage.output_tokens)
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
const client = new Anthropic();

const msg = await client.messages.create({
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  max_tokens: 1024,
  system: 'You are a concise assistant.',   // top-level, NOT a message role
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hello, Claude' }],
});

// content is a LIST OF BLOCKS. Never index [0] blindly.
for (const block of msg.content) {
  if (block.type === 'text') console.log(block.text);
}

console.log(msg.stop_reason);
console.log(msg.usage.input_tokens, msg.usage.output_tokens);
◆Four facts, four questions
  • system is a top-level parameter. A role:"system" entry returns 400.
  • content is a list of blocks. Indexing [0] breaks when thinking or tool_use blocks appear.
  • stop_reason arrives on a successful 200. It is not an error.
  • The API is stateless. You resend the whole conversation every turn.

On Claude 4.5+, if input plus max_tokens exceeds the window the API accepts the request and may return stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded". Also handle refusal.

Streaming

stream.ts — where usage lives, and the post-200 error
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain quantum tunneling."}],
) as stream:
    for event in stream:
        if event.type == "content_block_delta" and event.delta.type == "text_delta":
            print(event.delta.text, end="", flush=True)
        elif event.type == "message_delta":
            # final stop_reason and cumulative usage arrive HERE
            print("stop:", event.delta.stop_reason)
    final = stream.get_final_message()
const stream = await client.messages.stream({
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  max_tokens: 1024,
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Explain quantum tunneling.' }],
});

try {
  for await (const event of stream) {
    if (event.type === 'content_block_delta' && event.delta.type === 'text_delta') {
      process.stdout.write(event.delta.text);
    }
  }
} catch (err) {
  // an error event can arrive AFTER the 200. Decide what to do
  // with the partial output the user has already seen.
  console.error('mid-stream failure', err);
}
const finalMessage = await stream.finalMessage();
▲The one that catches people

The HTTP status commits before generation finishes, so an error event can arrive after a 200. Your dashboard shows all-green while users watch answers stop mid-sentence. Final usage and stop_reason arrive in message_delta, not message_start.

Tools

tools.py — the full round trip including is_error
tools = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get current weather for a location. Use when the user asks "
                   "about conditions, temperature, or forecast. Do NOT use for "
                   "historical climate data.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"location": {"type": "string",
                                    "description": "City name, e.g. 'Denver, CO'"}},
        "required": ["location"],
    },
}]

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris?"}]
resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=1024,
                              tools=tools, messages=messages)

while resp.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = []
    for block in resp.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            try:
                out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)      # YOUR code runs it
                results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                                "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": out})
            except Exception as e:
                # give the model something actionable, do not throw
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                "content": str(e), "is_error": True})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, messages=messages)
const tools = [{
  name: 'get_weather',
  description: 'Get current weather for a location. Use when the user asks about '
             + 'conditions or forecast. Do NOT use for historical climate data.',
  input_schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: { location: { type: 'string', description: "City, e.g. 'Denver, CO'" } },
    required: ['location'],
  },
}];

let messages = [{ role: 'user', content: 'Weather in Paris?' }];
let resp = await client.messages.create({ model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  max_tokens: 1024, tools, messages });

while (resp.stop_reason === 'tool_use') {
  messages.push({ role: 'assistant', content: resp.content });
  const results = [];
  for (const block of resp.content) {
    if (block.type === 'tool_use') {
      try {
        const out = await runTool(block.name, block.input);   // YOUR code runs it
        results.push({ type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: block.id, content: out });
      } catch (e) {
        results.push({ type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: block.id,
                       content: String(e), is_error: true });
      }
    }
  }
  messages.push({ role: 'user', content: results });
  resp = await client.messages.create({ model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
    max_tokens: 1024, tools, messages });
}

Every tool_use needs a matching tool_result in the next message, and tool_result blocks come before any text in that message. Add strict: true to a tool definition for guaranteed schema-valid inputs.

Caching

cache.py — prefix order and the timestamp anti-pattern
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    # PREFIX ORDER IS FIXED: tools, then system, then messages.
    system=[
        {"type": "text", "text": "You are a support assistant."},
        {"type": "text",
         "text": PRODUCT_DOCS,                        # large + stable
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},     # 5-minute rolling TTL
        # {"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}}  # 1-hour option
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
)

# Watch these two. A drop to zero means your prefix changed.
print("write:", resp.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)
print("read: ", resp.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)

# ANTI-PATTERN — this kills every cache hit forever:
#   {"type": "text", "text": f"Current time: {datetime.now()}"}   <-- never
# Anything interpolated inside the cached prefix makes each request unique.
const resp = await client.messages.create({
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  max_tokens: 1024,
  // PREFIX ORDER IS FIXED: tools, then system, then messages.
  system: [
    { type: 'text', text: 'You are a support assistant.' },
    { type: 'text',
      text: PRODUCT_DOCS,                          // large + stable
      cache_control: { type: 'ephemeral' } },      // 5-minute rolling TTL
  ],
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: question }],
});

console.log('write:', resp.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens);
console.log('read: ', resp.usage.cache_read_input_tokens);

// ANTI-PATTERN: any interpolated value inside the cached prefix
// (timestamp, session id, user name) makes every request unique.

Caching references the entire prompt in the order tools → system → messages, up to your breakpoint, and the match is exact. Reads are 0.1× base input, so a 5-minute cache pays for itself after one read and the 1-hour tier after two. Hits are not all-or-nothing across multiple breakpoints. Minimum cacheable granularity is around 1,024 tokens.

Batch

batch.py — 50% off, and why positional joins corrupt data
# 50% off. No streaming. Results come back OUT OF ORDER.
batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=[
    {"custom_id": f"doc-{i}",                    # 1-64 chars, your ONLY join key
     "params": {"model": "claude-sonnet-4-6", "max_tokens": 1024,
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": doc}]}}
    for i, doc in enumerate(documents)
])

import time
while True:
    b = client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id)
    if b.processing_status == "ended":
        break
    time.sleep(30)

# JOIN ON custom_id. Never zip positionally against your input list.
results = {}
for r in client.messages.batches.results(batch.id):
    if r.result.type == "succeeded":
        results[r.custom_id] = r.result.message
    elif r.result.type == "errored":
        retry_later.append(r.custom_id)   # individual failures inside a good batch
const batch = await client.messages.batches.create({
  requests: documents.map((doc, i) => ({
    custom_id: 'doc-' + i,               // 1-64 chars, your ONLY join key
    params: { model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6', max_tokens: 1024,
              messages: [{ role: 'user', content: doc }] },
  })),
});

let b;
do {
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 30000));
  b = await client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id);
} while (b.processing_status !== 'ended');

// JOIN ON custom_id. Never zip positionally against your input list.
const results = {};
for await (const r of client.messages.batches.results(batch.id)) {
  if (r.result.type === 'succeeded') results[r.custom_id] = r.result.message;
}

Up to 10,000 requests per batch, 24-hour window, results viewable for 29 days. No streaming. Individual requests can error inside an otherwise successful batch. Batch and cache discounts stack, though cache hits in batch are best-effort because requests process concurrently.

Vision, documents, and citations

documents.py — three ingestion methods and grounding
import base64, pathlib

pdf_b64 = base64.standard_b64encode(pathlib.Path("contract.pdf").read_bytes()).decode()

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=2048,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document",
         "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf",
                    "data": pdf_b64},
         "title": "contract.pdf",
         "citations": {"enabled": True}},        # grounds answers in real passages
        {"type": "text", "text": "List every payment milestone."},
    ]}],
)

# Three ingestion methods: url, base64, or Files API file_id.
# For anything reused, upload once and reference by file_id:
#   {"type": "document", "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": "file_abc123"}}
#
# Budget ~1500-3000 tokens per page. PDF support runs through VISION,
# so charts, tables and layout survive. .docx/.xlsx must be converted first.
import fs from 'node:fs';

const pdfB64 = fs.readFileSync('contract.pdf').toString('base64');

const resp = await client.messages.create({
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6', max_tokens: 2048,
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: [
    { type: 'document',
      source: { type: 'base64', media_type: 'application/pdf', data: pdfB64 },
      title: 'contract.pdf',
      citations: { enabled: true } },
    { type: 'text', text: 'List every payment milestone.' },
  ]}],
});

// For reused documents, upload once via the Files API and reference by file_id.
// Budget ~1500-3000 tokens per page; PDF support runs through vision.

Images consume tokens proportional to dimensions, so resizing is a real cost lever. PDF limits are 32MB and 100 pages for 200K-window models; 1M-window models accept up to 600 pages. Scanned PDFs without a text layer are not citable.

Thinking

effort.py — the new control surface
# CURRENT models: effort is the dial. Adaptive thinking is on by default.
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=8192,          # thinking eats this FIRST. Budget generously.
    effort="medium",          # low | medium | high (default) | xhigh | max
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
)

# 400 ON OPUS 5 / SONNET 5 -- all four of these:
#   temperature=0.7
#   top_p=0.9
#   thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 4000}
#   messages=[..., {"role": "assistant", "content": "{"}]   # prefill

# OLDER models (Sonnet 4.5 and earlier) still need the manual form:
# thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 4000}

# Thinking tokens bill at OUTPUT rates. Log them separately or your
# cost model will be quietly wrong.
const resp = await client.messages.create({
  model: 'claude-opus-5',
  max_tokens: 8192,      // thinking eats this FIRST
  effort: 'medium',      // low | medium | high (default) | xhigh | max
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: prompt }],
});

// 400 on Opus 5 / Sonnet 5:
//   temperature, top_p, top_k (non-default)
//   thinking: { type: 'enabled', budget_tokens: N }
//   assistant prefill
//
// Effort tuning is usually a better lever than swapping models:
// it preserves the behaviour you already evaluated.

Third-party vendors

Claude runs on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. Model IDs differ by platform, feature and beta availability lags first-party, and auth uses the provider's IAM rather than an Anthropic key. Regional endpoints are the answer when a stem names data residency; global endpoints route dynamically for availability, which is the opposite of what residency requires.

Realtime vs batch

◆The most repeated tradeoff in this domain

The deciding question is always: is anyone waiting for this result?
software-engineering-foundations:
Ordinary engineering practice applied to Claude work. Not distributed-systems resilience theory.

REST APIs — verbs, status semantics, headers, auth, idempotency, pagination. The Claude API is REST; the SDKs wrap it.
JSON — schema design, valid versus semantically correct, parsing failures.
Async — model calls are slow I/O. Bound your concurrency; unbounded fan-out produces 429s.
Version control — prompts, tool schemas, CLAUDE.md, and settings.json are all versioned artifacts.
SDLC integration — CI checks, eval runs as a release gate, staged environments.
Code review — review AI-generated code with the same rigour as human-written code. The human stays accountable for merged output.

errors.py — retries you already have
import anthropic, httpx

# SDKs ALREADY retry twice with exponential backoff, honouring retry-after.
# Do not wrap this in your own retry loop.
client = anthropic.Anthropic(
    max_retries=5,                                   # default 2, 0 disables
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(600.0, connect=30.0),      # default 10 minutes
)

try:
    msg = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}])
except anthropic.RateLimitError:
    pass          # 429 - RPM, input TPM, or output TPM. Shape concurrency.
except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:
    if e.status_code == 529:
        pass      # overloaded, transient, back off
    elif e.status_code == 400:
        raise     # malformed or unsupported param. Retrying is pointless.
except anthropic.APIConnectionError as e:
    print("unreachable", e.__cause__)

# Per-request override:
# client.with_options(max_retries=0).messages.create(...)
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';

// SDKs ALREADY retry twice with exponential backoff, honouring retry-after.
const client = new Anthropic({
  maxRetries: 5,        // default 2, 0 disables
  timeout: 600 * 1000,  // default 10 minutes
});

try {
  await client.messages.create({ model: 'claude-opus-5', max_tokens: 1024,
    messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }] });
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof Anthropic.RateLimitError) {
    // 429 - RPM, input TPM, or output TPM
  } else if (err instanceof Anthropic.APIStatusError && err.status === 529) {
    // overloaded, transient
  } else if (err instanceof Anthropic.APIStatusError && err.status === 400) {
    throw err;   // malformed or unsupported param. Retrying is pointless.
  }
}
▲The retry trap

SDKs retry connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx twice by default with exponential backoff, honouring retry-after. A hand-rolled fixed-delay retry on top multiplies request volume during exactly the incident it was meant to survive. Non-retryable: 400, 401, 403, 404, 413.

Refactoring, small- and large-scale

Explicitly named, and it connects to Claude Code for codebase modernization. Small-scale: rename, extract, simplify, tighten types. Large-scale: module boundaries, dependency inversion, framework migration, strangler-fig.

✦With Claude specifically

Work in bounded increments with tests green between each. Never refactor and add behaviour in the same change. Tests are the safety net that makes automated refactoring trustworthy; without them you're gambling.
claude-application-design:
★Heaviest single objective on the exam

This is about how instructions are interpreted and how sessions and content stay clean. Workflow pattern selection is Domain 1, not here.

Instruction interpretation across interfaces

InterfaceInstruction surfaceCharacter
Claude APIsystem, user messages, tool descriptionsMost direct. Stateless. You control everything
Client SDKsSame, plus SDK defaultsRetries, streaming helpers, typing over the same REST surface
Claude CodeCLAUDE.md, settings.json, Rules, Skills, commandsLayered and merged. Precedence matters
Claude DesktopConnected MCP servers, local configInstruction surface is the connected tooling
claude.aiProjects, project instructions, knowledge, StylesUI configuration, no code-level control
◆The testable principle

Choose the surface whose durability matches the requirement. Every session in a repo → CLAUDE.md. Every API request → system. Must be enforced rather than followed → a hook.

Content boundaries

  • Instructions in system; untrusted data in user turns or tool results
  • Delimit untrusted content explicitly so the model can tell data from instruction
  • Never concatenate user input into the system prompt. It collapses the trust boundary and breaks caching
  • Retrieved documents, web pages, file contents, tool outputs, and MCP responses are all untrusted

Schema design

structured.py — nullable fields let the model decline
# Structured outputs replace the deprecated assistant-prefill trick.
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Extract fields from: {text}"}],
    extra_headers={"anthropic-beta": "structured-outputs-2025-11-13"},
    extra_body={"output_format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "vendor": {"type": "string"},
            # nullable so the model can DECLINE instead of fabricating
            "contract_end_date": {"type": ["string", "null"]},
            "status": {"type": "string", "enum": ["active", "expired", "pending"]},
        },
        "required": ["vendor", "contract_end_date", "status"],
    }}},
)

import json
# still check stop_reason before parsing - max_tokens truncation
# produces invalid JSON that no repair loop can fix
if resp.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
    raise ValueError("truncated: raise budget or decompose the task")
data = json.loads(resp.content[0].text)
const resp = await client.messages.create({
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  max_tokens: 1024,
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Extract fields from: ' + text }],
  betas: ['structured-outputs-2025-11-13'],
  output_format: { type: 'json_schema', schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      vendor: { type: 'string' },
      contract_end_date: { type: ['string', 'null'] },  // nullable = can decline
      status: { type: 'string', enum: ['active', 'expired', 'pending'] },
    },
    required: ['vendor', 'contract_end_date', 'status'],
  }},
});

if (resp.stop_reason === 'max_tokens')
  throw new Error('truncated: raise budget or decompose');

Descriptive field names beat terse ones; the model reads them as documentation. Enums where the value set is closed. Keep schemas small — every field is tokens and a chance to hallucinate. Validate on receipt regardless; schema-valid and semantically correct are different things.

Session hygiene

  • Start fresh when the task changes. Carrying unrelated context degrades quality and wastes tokens
  • Don't let one long session accumulate contradictory instructions
  • Session boundaries are security boundaries — never carry one tenant's context into another's
  • Isolate exploratory or high-volume subtasks into subagents so the main session stays clean

Plugin management

Plugins bundle commands, skills, agents, and MCP servers into an installable unit. Manage them as dependencies. Every plugin expands the tool surface and the trust surface: more tokens on definitions per request, and more chance of the wrong tool being selected.
configuration-management:
CLAUDE.md

Loaded automatically. Hierarchical: enterprise → user → project → subdirectory, merged with more specific levels layering on. Committed so the team shares it.

settings.json

.claude/settings.json is shared and committed. .claude/settings.local.json is personal and gitignored. ~/.claude/settings.json is user level. Anything protecting production belongs in the shared file so a teammate can't silently disable it.

Model version pinning

▲The signature failure

Quality shifts on a day nothing shipped, with no deploy and no prompt change. That's an unpinned alias letting the underlying model move beneath you. Pin explicit dated IDs in production and gate upgrades on an eval re-run. Moving the alias into an environment variable relocates the config without stopping the drift.

Prompt versioning — prompts are code: version control, review, semantic versions, eval results tied to each version, rollback as fast as a code rollback.
Plugin dependencies — pin plugin and MCP server versions; treat an update like any dependency bump.

◈Boundary

Environment separation lives here. Secrets management itself is Domain 7, not this objective.
claude-code-operation:
ComponentWhat it is
RulesPersistent instructions governing behaviour in a project
SkillsFolders of instructions and resources loaded on demand
CommandsReusable prompts as slash commands in .claude/commands/
AgentsSubagents with own context, prompt, tool permissions, in .claude/agents/
Agent MemoryPersistent context across sessions

Features: session management, built-in and custom slash commands (/init, /clear, /model, /agents), headless mode via -p for CI with a JSON output format, streaming mode, and auto-mode (reduced approval prompting, real risk, scope it tightly).

Authoring a Skill

SKILL.md — frontmatter is the trigger
---
name: brand-voice-check
description: Checks markdown files in drafts/ for forbidden brand phrases and
  passive voice before publication. Use when reviewing or editing any draft
  article, blog post, or marketing page.
---

# Brand Voice Check

## When to run
Any time a file under drafts/ is edited or the user asks for a voice review.

## Procedure
1. Read the file.
2. Flag every phrase in references/forbidden.md.
3. Flag passive constructions.
4. Report as a table: line number, issue, suggested rewrite.

## Notes
Never rewrite silently. Always show the user what changed and why.
◆Description-as-trigger

Claude decides whether to load a Skill by reading its description, so it works like a search query. name is capped around 64 chars, lowercase-hyphen, matching the folder. description is capped around 1024 chars and must say what it does AND when to use it. Vague descriptions fire on everything.

Progressive disclosure is the design principle: metadata (~100 tokens) always loaded, SKILL.md body (under ~5k tokens) loaded on trigger, bundled resources loaded as needed. That's what makes a large Skill library affordable. Keep the body under about 500 lines, and avoid angle-bracket tags — they're an injection risk.

✦Four surfaces, four answers

CLAUDE.md for memory. Skills for routines. Hooks for guarantees. Subagents for delegation. If you're writing "Claude must always" or "Claude should never," that's a hook, not a CLAUDE.md line.
debugging-and-error-handling:
Error type identification

CodeMeansRecovery
400Malformed, or param unsupported on that modelFix the request. Retrying is pointless
401 / 403Bad key, or key lacks accessCredentials
404Often a retired model IDCheck the deprecation list
413Payload over limitFiles API, or split
429RPM / input TPM / output TPM, or acceleration limitsBackoff, shape concurrency
529OverloadedBackoff and retry

Not errors: stop_reason: max_tokens and refusal arrive on a 200. Truncation means raise the budget or decompose — never send truncated output back for repair, because the missing content was never generated and a repair loop asks the model to invent it.

◆The core diagnostic question

Raw output correct but the app misbehaves → integration layer (parsing, block indexing, joins).
Raw output wrong → model layer (prompt, context, schema, model choice).
Always inspect the raw response before blaming the model.

Evals, testing, and production monitoring

◈Why this is here

The domain is titled Eval, Testing, and Debugging, and the guide's competency list names designing and running evals, validating structured output, and monitoring production quality. Lightly scored here and load-bearing everywhere: model selection is decided by evals, prompt tuning is gated on them, migrations are cleared by them.

Grading methods, cheapest first

MethodUse whenWatch for
Code-based exact matchClassification, extraction, one right answerCheapest and most reliable. Use it wherever it fits
Schema validationStructured outputProves shape, says nothing about correctness
Similarity scoringSummaries with expected contentBlunt. Misses correct rewordings
LLM-as-judgeOpen-ended quality, tone, reasoningNeeds its own rubric and its own validation
Human reviewHigh-stakes, judge calibrationSlowest. Reserve it
▲Validating a judge

Anthropic's guidance is that LLM judges must be closely calibrated with human experts. A judge produces consistent scores whether or not it measures what you care about — consistency is not accuracy. Run it across a labelled golden set and measure agreement (Cohen's Kappa, precision/recall). The MT-Bench research found strong judges reach agreement with humans comparable to human-to-human agreement, which is the bar, not a free pass. Grade each dimension with its own judge rather than one judge for everything, and give the judge an "Unknown" option so it can decline.

Monitoring production quality

  • Instrument every request: model, all token counts including cache and thinking, latency, stop_reason, tool sequence, error type
  • Quality signals: schema failure rate, refusal rate, truncation rate, retry rate, tool error rate, user corrections
  • Alert on drift, not just failure. Requests returning 200 while quality degrades is the failure no error dashboard catches
  • Sample production failures back into the eval set. They're the highest-value test cases you'll ever get
llm-fundamentals:
Tokens — roughly 4 characters or 0.75 words in English. Code and non-English text are denser. Counts are model-specific; re-measure on migration.

Context window — everything the model references for one request. Distinct from max output tokens, which is a separate limit. Advertised context is not effective context: quality degrades as the window fills.

Next-token generation — output is sequential, so output tokens cost roughly 5× input and latency tracks output length far more than input length.

count.py — ask before you send
# Ask before you send.
count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    system=SYSTEM,
    tools=TOOLS,
    messages=messages,
)
print(count.input_tokens)

# Query limits instead of hardcoding them.
for m in client.models.list():
    print(m.id, m.max_input_tokens, m.max_tokens)

# Token counts are MODEL-SPECIFIC. Re-measure after any migration -
# 4.7+ use a newer tokenizer producing ~30% more tokens for the same text.
const count = await client.messages.countTokens({
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  system: SYSTEM,
  tools: TOOLS,
  messages,
});
console.log(count.input_tokens);

for await (const m of client.models.list()) {
  console.log(m.id, m.max_input_tokens, m.max_tokens);
}

Sampling — temperature, top_p, top_k. Note current 5-series models reject non-default sampling parameters with a 400; effort has replaced them.

Model options

OptionWhat it does
Fast modeLatency-optimized execution. Research preview on Opus 5 / 4.8
Extended thinkingExplicit reasoning budget. Sonnet 4.5 and earlier only
Adaptive thinkingModel decides per step. Default on 4.6+; the only mode on 4.7+
Effortlow / medium / high (default) / xhigh / max. A behavioural signal, not a token cap
◈Placement trap

Zero-shot, single-shot, and multi-shot prompting are scored here in Domain 5, not in Domain 6. More examples help up to a point; diverse examples covering edge cases beat many similar ones. The example block costs input tokens on every call, which is why it belongs inside the cached prefix.
technical-fundamentals:
▲Narrower than it sounds

The objective scopes this as basic engineering practice for AI application development: SDKs that wrap REST APIs, and websockets. Not context window theory or rate limit mechanics.

What the SDK adds over raw HTTP

  • Typed request/response models
  • Automatic retries — twice by default, exponential backoff, honours retry-after, configurable via max retries
  • Streaming helpers that assemble SSE events into usable objects
  • Timeout handling (10-minute default) and connection reuse
  • Pagination helpers, and a request ID on responses for support

Go raw HTTP only when you're in an unsupported language or need precise transport control — and you inherit retries, backoff, SSE parsing, and timeouts. Pricing and auth are unchanged.

Websockets vs SSE vs request/response

TransportDirectionFits
Request/responseOne shotStandard API calls
SSEServer → clientWhat Claude API streaming uses
WebSocketFull duplexYour own client when it also sends mid-stream: cancel, interrupt, voice

Common architecture: WebSocket between browser and your server, SSE between your server and the Claude API. Know that Claude streaming is SSE; a websocket is something you add in your own transport layer.
model-selection-and-tradeoffs:
TierShapeReach for it when
HaikuFastest, cheapest, 200K context, no effort supportHigh-volume, latency-sensitive, narrow: classification, routing, extraction, moderation
SonnetBest balance of intelligence and speedThe default for most production work
OpusHardest reasoning, highest cost and latencyComplex coding, deep analysis, long agentic chains
Fable / MythosAbove Opus. Thinking always onMaximum capability
◆Explicitly in the blueprint

Adaptive thinking support differs by tier. Haiku uses explicit extended thinking and has no effort parameter. It's a differently shaped model, not just a cheaper one.

Two valid selection strategies, and the stem tells you which: start cheap and escalate when evals miss the bar (best when volume is high), or start capable and optimize down while evals hold (best when feasibility is the open question). Evals decide, not intuition.

✦The lever most people miss

Effort tuning is usually better than a model swap. Stepping effort down preserves the model behaviour you already evaluated; swapping tiers invalidates every eval you've run.

Breaking behaviour changes across releases

Named explicitly in this objective. The durable idea is the one to hold: a model swap can break working code, so a migration is gated on a documentation read and an eval re-run, never on editing the model string alone.

▲Confidence note

The specifics below are accurate as of August 2026 but post-date the exam guide (v1.0, July 2026). Items were written against the lineup that existed then, so treat this as engineering knowledge rather than exam content. Learn the pattern; skim the list.

  • Manual thinking budgets rejected once a model moves to adaptive thinking
  • Non-default temperature, top_p, top_k rejected on the newest models; effort replaced them
  • Assistant prefill rejected; structured outputs replaced it
  • Legacy beta headers removed, so they must be stripped on migration
  • Context window and max output limits change between generations
◈Two silent traps worth knowing

Tokenizer changes. Newer models can produce meaningfully more tokens for identical text, so effective cost per request rises even when the headline rate is flat. Re-run token counting after any migration.

max_tokens carryover. Where thinking is on by default, reasoning consumes the budget before the visible answer starts. A tight max_tokens copied from an older model truncates responses for no obvious reason.
cost-and-token-management:
Optimization order — cheapest effort first

  1. Send fewer tokens. Trim the prompt, retrieve less, compact history
  2. Prompt caching on any stable prefix
  3. Batch for anything latency-tolerant (scored in Domain 2)
  4. Effort step-down on the same model
  5. Model downgrade — last, because it invalidates your evals
▲The classic mistake

Reaching for step 5 first. A scenario will dramatize this: a team proposing a tier downgrade when a cache breakpoint and an effort step would have fixed it without touching validated behaviour.

Cache check-pointing

Place breakpoints at stability boundaries — after tools, after the system prompt, after static documents. Order content most stable first so a late change doesn't invalidate everything behind it. In growing conversations, a breakpoint on the latest turn lets history cache incrementally.

Tracking

Log input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, and thinking tokens separately, attributed per feature and per tenant. Alert on cost-per-transaction drift, not monthly totals. Don't ship a global max-effort flag — that's the Opus-for-everything mistake in a different hat.

What the tiers cost

Per million tokens, August 2026. Learn the ratios rather than the digits: naming moves fast and the relationships are what get tested.

TierInputOutputCache read
Frontier (Fable)$10$50$1
Opus$5$25$0.50
Sonnet$2$10$0.20
Haiku$1$5$0.10

Output runs roughly 5× input at every tier. Cache reads are about a tenth of input, and cache writes are 1.25× at the 5-minute TTL or 2× at one hour — so a 5-minute cache pays for itself after a single read and the 1-hour tier after two. Batch is 50% off in both directions and stacks with caching.
context-engineering:
Anthropic frames context as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns — recall degrades as the window fills, sometimes called context rot. Budget deliberately: system prompt + tools + retrieved content + history + reserved output space.

Drift vs bloat

Context drift is behaviour degrading as original instructions get diluted or contradicted. Fix by restating key constraints, keeping instructions in the stable system layer, and starting fresh at task boundaries.

Context bloat is the window filling with low-value tokens. Two named mitigations:

  • Tool output pruning — truncate, summarize, or filter verbose results before they enter context. A 40k-token API dump should become a 200-token summary. Usually the single largest source of bloat in agentic systems
  • Compaction — summarize older turns and replace them
◈Compaction's real tradeoff

It is lossy. What survives is a design decision, not an automatic behaviour. Decisions and outcomes should survive; transcript detail usually shouldn't.

Context isolation — push high-volume or exploratory work into subagents so raw material never enters the parent context. Only the distilled result returns.

✦The "right altitude" idea

Anthropic's guidance on system prompts: specific enough to guide, flexible enough to leave heuristics. Avoid brittle if-else prompt logic at one extreme and vague guidance at the other. Use XML tags or Markdown headers to delineate sections.
prompt-engineering:
• Instruction clarity — explicit beats clever. State what to do, not just what to avoid. Ambiguity is where non-determinism does the most damage
  • Few-shot examples — demonstrate format and edge cases. Curate diverse canonical examples rather than stuffing every edge case
  • System vs user placement — durable role and constraints in system; task and data in the user turn. Per-request data in system breaks caching and blurs the trust boundary
  • Output constraints — prefer structured outputs or a tool schema over asking politely for JSON
  • Placement across components — the same instruction lands differently in system, a user turn, a tool description, CLAUDE.md, or a hook. Tool descriptions are prompts
  • Iterative refinement — change one thing, re-run the eval set, keep or revert
  • Input sanitization — neutralize injected instructions in untrusted input, delimit clearly, never interpolate raw user input into the instruction layer
◆Why the eval set comes first

A prompt edit that fixes one case commonly regresses three others. Without an eval set you can't see the trade you just made — you only see the case you were looking at.
output-handling:
• Structured output patterns — the structured outputs feature or a tool schema, not prose instructions
  • Response validation — validate against the schema and check semantic plausibility. Schema-valid nonsense is still nonsense
  • Defensive parsing — iterate blocks by type, check stop_reason before parsing, handle truncation and unexpected block types
  • Skepticism toward confident output — fluency is not accuracy, and the model expresses uncertainty poorly
✦Structural mitigations for overconfidence

Require citations to provided context. Make fields nullable so "unknown" is representable. Cross-check high-stakes values against a source of truth. Gate consequential actions behind human review. Asking the model to confirm its own answer is not independent verification.
ai-application-security:
Direct injection is where the user is the adversary. Indirect injection is where a trusted user brings adversarial third-party content — a web page, a document, an email, a tool result. Indirect is the harder case and the one scenarios use.

✓What works — structural
  • Separate trusted instructions from untrusted content; delimit explicitly
  • Least privilege on tools — an injection can only do what the tools allow, so the permission set is the real control
  • Human approval on consequential or irreversible actions
  • Hooks that deterministically block dangerous operations
  • Screening with a cheap fast model before the main call
  • Sandboxed tool execution and narrowly scoped permissions
✕What doesn't — the four classic distractors
  • Asking users not to inject
  • Adding "ignore malicious instructions" to the system prompt — not an enforceable control
  • Changing temperature — irrelevant to injection
  • Switching to a bigger model — better instruction-following can make injection more effective, not less
◈The recursive trap

A guardrail LLM is itself injectable. If you screen input with a general chat model, that screen can be talked out of screening. Purpose-trained classifiers are the sturdier option.

Integrity

The objective lists integrity alongside authentication, authorisation, confidentiality, and privacy, and it is the one people skip. Integrity is assurance that data and instructions have not been altered by anyone unauthorised to alter them. In a Claude system it fails in specific ways:

  • Instruction integrity — injected text in retrieved content altering behaviour. This is why content boundaries are an integrity control, not just a safety one
  • Memory and context integrity — poisoned agent memory persisting a false fact into every future session
  • Output integrity — a fabricated value flowing into a system of record because nothing validated it
  • Supply-chain integrity — an unpinned plugin or MCP server changing behaviour beneath you

The controls are validation on receipt, pinned dependencies, audit logs, and never letting unvalidated model output become a durable record.

Data leakage — don't put secrets in prompts (they can be echoed); scope retrieval to what the current user may see; filter output before it crosses a boundary; never let one tenant's cached prefix or session context reach another.

◆AuthN / AuthZ

Authenticate the user, authorize per-user at the tool boundary, never rely on the model to enforce access control. The model asking to call a tool is not authorization to execute it. Your harness authorizes.
guardrails-and-safe-deployment:
Guardrail layering — input guardrails (screening, sanitization), in-flight (system constraints, tool permissions), output (validation, filtering, classifiers), and human review gates. Layers stay independent so one failure isn't total.

◆The agent permission rule

An agent acts on behalf of a user and inherits that user's permissions, never a superset. Entitlement is verified at the tool boundary on each request — a session-start check misses mid-session permission changes. Scope per task rather than per role.

Named agent-specific threats worth recognizing: prompt injection, tool poisoning, identity and privilege abuse, memory poisoning, and supply-chain attacks through installed tooling.

Deployment practice: staged rollout, feature flags, kill switch, monitoring for anomalous tool use, incident response plan, and audit trails.
claude-hooks:
◆The central idea

A prompt instruction is a request. A hook is a control. Hooks are deterministic code at fixed lifecycle points. Anything that must happen every time belongs in one.

settings.json + guard.sh — the blocking pattern
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks/guard.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .claude/hooks/guard.sh
input=$(cat)                       # hook payload arrives on stdin as JSON
command=$(printf '%s' "$input" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // ""')

if printf '%s' "$command" | grep -qiE '(^|[[:space:]])rm[[:space:]]+(-[a-z]*r|--recursive)'; then
  echo "Recursive rm is blocked by project policy." >&2
  exit 2      # EXIT 2 BLOCKS. stderr goes back to Claude as the reason.
fi

exit 0        # exit 0 proceeds. exit 1 is a NON-BLOCKING error - the footgun.
EventFiresCan block?
PreToolUseAfter parameters are built, before the tool runsYes — the guardrail event
PostToolUseAfter the tool runsNo. Cannot undo. Formatting, logging, feedback
UserPromptSubmitOn prompt submissionYes
SessionStartSession beginsContext injection
Stop / SubagentStopAgent finishesYes — can prevent stopping
▲Exit codes are the whole game

Exit 2 blocks and stderr goes back to Claude as the reason. Exit 0 proceeds. Exit 1 is a non-blocking error — the action still runs. That's the biggest footgun in hooks: a crashing guard script fails open, not closed. Alternatively exit 0 with JSON carrying a permission decision of allow, deny, or ask.

Matchers are case-sensitive regex against the tool name, not prompt text. Hooks run as real code with your permissions — quote your variables, and prefer grep over eval on anything the model generated.
identity-secrets-and-key-management:
• Keys from a secret manager, injected at runtime. Never in source, client-side code, CLAUDE.md, a committed config, or logs
  • Separate keys per environment, service, and tenant where it matters — separate blast radius, separate revocation
  • Rotation on schedule and on suspicion. Design so rotation doesn't require a deploy
  • Workspace-scoped keys with spend limits
  • Identity validation — authenticate the human, not just the service
  • Access approval and level verification at the tool boundary, per request
  • Monitoring — log who invoked what, with which identity, against which resource
▲Client-side keys

A key shipped to a browser or mobile app is compromised the moment it ships, and obfuscation only delays extraction. Proxy through your backend, which also gives you a place to enforce per-user authorization and rate limiting.
tool-implementation:
◆Tool descriptions are prompts

Anthropic's guidance is blunt: tool definitions deserve as much prompt engineering attention as your main prompt. The model selects tools by reading name, description, and schema. If a human engineer can't say definitively which tool applies in a situation, the model can't either.

  • Say what the tool does, when to use it, and when not to
  • Name parameters unambiguously — user_id, not user
  • Document units and formats; note side effects and irreversibility
  • Return context-efficient results. Claude Code caps tool responses around 25,000 tokens by default; use pagination, filtering, or truncation

Configuration for external system interaction

Named explicitly in this objective and easy to overlook. A tool is not just a schema; it is a configured connection to something real.

  • Endpoints and environments — the same tool points at different hosts in dev, staging, and production. That mapping is configuration, not code
  • Credentials — each external system needs its own, from a secret manager, scoped to the least it needs, never in the tool definition the model can read
  • Timeouts and retries — a slow downstream service must not hang the agent loop. Set a per-tool timeout well inside your overall budget
  • Rate limits — the external system has its own, separate from Anthropic's. An agent that retries eagerly will find them
  • Identity propagation — the call should carry the end user's identity, not a shared service account, so authorisation happens against the real requester

Tool error handling

Return errors as a tool_result with the error flag and an actionable message — "customer_id not found; expected format CUST-XXXXX" — rather than throwing. The model can then correct and retry. Never leak stack traces or connection strings back into context.

Usage patterns

  • Agentic harness dispatch — routes tool_use blocks to implementations, enforces permissions, executes in parallel where safe
  • Client-side vs server-side — client-side means your code executes (databases, internal APIs, filesystem); server-side means Anthropic's infrastructure executes (web search, code execution)
  • Approval patterns — auto-approve read-only, confirm on writes and irreversible operations, allowlist by tool and argument pattern. Remember approval fatigue causes blanket-approving

Tool set construction: fewer, well-chosen tools beat many overlapping ones. Every definition costs tokens on every request and adds selection ambiguity. Idempotency on anything that writes, because agents retry.
mcp-server-development:
An open protocol standardizing how applications expose context and tools to models. Build once, connect to many clients. JSON-RPC 2.0 underneath.

server.py — three primitives, one file
# pip install mcp
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("inventory-server")

@mcp.tool()                              # MODEL-controlled: an action
def check_stock(sku: str) -> int:
    """Return current stock level for a SKU."""
    return db.stock(sku)

@mcp.resource("catalog://{category}")    # APP-controlled: read-only data
def catalog(category: str) -> str:
    return db.catalog(category)

@mcp.prompt()                            # USER-controlled: a template
def restock_review(sku: str) -> str:
    return f"Review restocking needs for {sku}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()                            # stdio by default (local, no network)
    # mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
// npm i @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod
import { McpServer } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js';
import { StdioServerTransport } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js';
import { z } from 'zod';

const server = new McpServer({ name: 'inventory-server', version: '1.0.0' });

server.registerTool('check_stock',
  { inputSchema: { sku: z.string() } },
  async ({ sku }) => ({ content: [{ type: 'text', text: String(db.stock(sku)) }] }));

const transport = new StdioServerTransport();
await server.connect(transport);

// Transport heuristic: docs give you a COMMAND -> stdio.
//                      docs give you a URL     -> streamable HTTP.
// HTTP+SSE is deprecated. Streamable HTTP needs OAuth 2.1.
PrimitiveControlled byPurpose
ToolsModelActions the model can invoke
ResourcesApplicationRead-only data pulled into context
PromptsUserReusable templates the user invokes
◈Transport heuristic

Docs give you a command to run → stdio, local, no network exposure. Docs give you a URL → Streamable HTTP, the current standard, needs OAuth 2.1. HTTP+SSE is deprecated. That one rule answers most transport questions.

A host runs one client per connected server. Connections open with an initialize handshake negotiating capabilities — a client can't use what wasn't negotiated.

▲MCP security in 2026

Dozens of MCP-related CVEs surfaced in early 2026. Validate Origin headers on HTTP servers, keep authorization in the server scoped to the calling identity, and treat an installed MCP server as a supply-chain dependency.

◆The stem signal

When a scenario says the capability must be reusable across multiple applications and maintained independently, that's an MCP server. Those two phrases together are the tell.
agentic-customization:
Larger than MCP development itself, and the most likely place Domain 8 gets tested.

ApproachWhat it isChoose when
Built-in toolsAnthropic-provided: web search, code execution, text editor, bashThe capability already exists. Don't rebuild it
Custom toolsFunction schemas you define, executed by your codeA specific action inside one app, tightly coupled to it
SkillsFolders of instructions and resources, loaded on demandTeaching procedure and knowledge, not adding capability
MCP serversStandalone servers exposing tools, resources, promptsReuse across applications, maintained independently
◆Skill vs tool

A Skill changes how Claude does something it can already do. A tool gives it a new capability. "Follow our code review checklist" is a Skill. "Query the inventory database" is a tool. Skills and MCP are complements: Skills carry knowledge and procedure, MCP carries integrated actions.

  • Custom tool vs MCP server — reuse and independent maintenance. One app, tightly coupled → custom tool. Many apps, own lifecycle → MCP server
  • Subagent vs Skill — a subagent gets its own context window and tool permissions; a Skill loads into the current conversation. Need separate context or different tools? Subagent
  • Cost — every tool and server adds definitions to every request
